# Battle of Drniš

Battle of Drniš was a military conflict between the SAO Krajina, supported by the Yugoslav People's Army and the local Territorial Defense, against the Croatian National Guard and Croatian Police. The fighting lasted from 16 September until the capture of Drniš on 21 September.
Background
In 1990, ethnic tensions between Serbs and Croats worsened after the electoral defeat of the Socialist Republic of Croatia government by the Croatian Democratic Union. The Yugoslav People's Army disarmed the Territorial Defense of Croatia in order to minimize resistance. On 17 August, tensions escalated into an open rebellion by Croatian Serbs, centered in the predominantly Serb-populated areas of the Dalmatian hinterland around Knin (approximately 60 kilometres northeast of Split), parts of Lika, Kordun, Banovina, and eastern Croatia. In January 1991, Serbia, with the support of Montenegro and the Serbian provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo, unsuccessfully attempted to obtain approval from the Presidency of Yugoslavia for a JNA operation to disarm Croatian security forces. The request was rejected, and a bloodless clash between Serbian rebels and Croatian special police in March prompted the JNA itself to ask the federal president to grant it war powers and declare a state of emergency. Although the request was supported by Serbia and its allies, the JNA's request was rejected on 15 March. Serbian President Slobodan Milošević preferred a campaign for Serbian expansion to preserving Yugoslavia with Croatia as a federal unit, publicly threatened to replace the JNA with the Serbian army, and declared that he no longer recognized the authority of the federal presidency. The threat led the JNA to abandon plans to preserve Yugoslavia in favor of Serbian expansion, as the JNA came under Milošević's control. By the end of March, the conflict had escalated to the point of first casualties. In early April, the leaders of the Serbian rebellion in Croatia declared their intention to unite the areas under their control with Serbia. The Croatian government considered them separatist regions.In the beginning of the war, in 1991, Atif Dudaković was in Zadar, after which he moved to Knin. There he was given the rank of captain and the post of artillery commander under the command of Ratko Mladić.
The battle
On 16 September, the JNA, with the support of local Territorial Defense units, carried out three attacks, towards the city of Zadar and two smaller breakthroughs towards Šibenik and Drniš. JNA and Territorial Defense forces launched an attack with tanks, artillery and rocket launchers on the villages of Gradac, Otavice, Kadine Glave, Siverić, Lišnjak, Trbounje, Razvođe, Bogatić, etc., with the aim of capturing them and breaking through to the outskirts of Drniš. JNA and TO Krajina forces quickly captured the approaches to Drniš on 16 September. On the night of September 16 to 17, 1991, a column of Croatian civilians fled to Zagora. Women, children, the elderly and the sick walked across Čikola to Pakova Selo and Pokrovnik, and further by train and bus to safer places on the coast, about 17,000 Croatian civilians fled the area. Serbian forces captured the crossroads around the village of Oklaj on 18 September. The 114th Split Brigade of the Croatian National Army could do little to counter the JNA's armored vehicles and artillery. By 21 September, JNA forces and the Krajina TO had captured the town of Drniš itself.
Aftermath
JNA troops from the 22nd Regiment attacked Croatian forces around Sinj, opening the way for the Corps' Engineering Regiment to withdraw from the barracks. The Croats allowed the withdrawal on 27 September 1991.
